question: Can a woman marry without her father's permission if she believes his objection is unreasonable?
asked: I want to marry a brother I met on campus. We have feelings for each other but have kept ourselves pure for marriage. My father objects and won't allow it, and I feel his objections are unreasonable. I am an adult and can legally marry him under British law. If I am certain his objections are unreasonable, may I go ahead with the marriage?
answer:
Brothers and sisters, understand that the Sharia has placed a wali for a very simple reason, and that is to protect the interests of the lady. And I understand that some people think this is paternalistic, some people think this is misogynistic, some people think whatever. But at the end of the day, the Sharia is very clear on this point, and this is the position of the vast majority of ulama. And frankly, it is basic human psychology that a young lady who has never experienced men, never experienced any marriage, any long-term relationship with another man, can be taken advantage of. Not because she's naive; it's because she's innocent, and men are not innocent.

So rather than looking at it as a negative, we should look at it in a very different way: the Sharia is actually impugning men and the nature of men. The Sharia is saying: look, we're not too certain about any man that might be interested in a lady who doesn't have experience. And that's why, dear brothers and sisters, the Sharia has a different ruling on widows and on divorcees. Widows and divorcees: once you've been married to a man, once you know male psychology, at this stage the wali becomes a token, a rubber stamp; the wali does not have veto power. Once a woman understands the psychology of a man, inshallah she will not be fooled that easily. I mean, anybody can be fooled, man or woman. But when she has never lived with a man, known a man, and she has never been married before, the Sharia views a woman as being too pure and too innocent, and a wolf in sheep's clothing might want to take advantage of her.

And that is why the wali is placed, and that's literally what a wali means: a guardian. What does a guardian do? A guardian protects. A guardian makes sure that whatever is going to happen will be in the best interest of the young lady. And that is why the Sharia insists (this is the majority opinion; of course, one madhhab does not, but of course the majority, and the hadith mention it) that there should be a wali.

Now, what if the wali is being unreasonable? In this case, if you're living in an Islamic land, or in an ideal situation, you would go to an Islamic court. You would petition; you would say, "My father is being unjust. He is denying somebody's hand, and I think it is unfair." And so a third party, a neutral party, will look and will examine who is really more in the right, the plaintiff, the accusing party, or the defendant. And in that case it is possible that the judge will rule, "Okay, the father's wilayah is taken away," because he's being unreasonable for whatever reason.

However, generally speaking, and the sister is in London, we are not in such a situation. Therefore, in this situation, what I advise the sister is that she should go to a shaykh or an imam or a scholar who has experience in these issues. Not just anybody, because again, this is one of our problems: not everybody who has graduated from a madrasa becomes qualified to do everything. Go to a senior person of age and wisdom and experience, of community service, whose reputation is known. And another point (you might be shocked that I say this): go to somebody of your own culture. I think this is a very important point as well, because within one's own culture there are cultural nuances when it comes to this issue of wilayah that people outside the culture will not understand. Go to somebody in your locality of experience and wisdom and age, and somebody of your own background and culture, so that that person can understand what is going on and be better situated to assess how just or unjust your father is being. And then that imam or that shaykh can, if need be, contact your father, see what is going on, hear from him directly.

And look, if it is clear that he is being unreasonable... I'll give you a simple example. If he says, "I don't want a religious person to marry my daughter. Anybody who's praying five times a day, has a beard, whatnot, I don't want that person to marry my daughter," subhanAllah, in this case it is very clear, an open-and-shut case basically. If this were to happen to me and the man said this to me, I would say, "Okay, well, that is your prerogative to feel that way legally, and it is her prerogative in this land to get married legally." And I would interview the young man, see if he's religious and whatnot, and based on my assessment, inshallah, then maybe allow the marriage to take place.

However (and again, this might shock some of you, but it is a reality and a fact), if the man says, "I don't want somebody who doesn't have a job. I don't want somebody who's still in school. I want to marry my daughter off to somebody who has a good income," and he says a reasonable income, so if he's middle class and he's saying, "I want somebody of the same background," subhanAllah, this is not unreasonable at all. On the contrary, this is the essence of being reasonable; this is the essence of what a wali should do.

Again, I will shock some of you, and I will say: what if he says, "Oh, I want somebody from my cultural background"? Okay, by unanimous consensus of all of the madhahib, he has the right to place that condition, and it is a reasonable condition. It is not unreasonable. Why? Because when you marry, it's not just a business transaction. It's lifelong; you're adding somebody to your family. And you might want somebody to speak your language with, to have your cultural mannerisms with, to enjoy your own extended family. You want to have somebody of your own. This is not haram; it's not at all racism. On the contrary, anybody who says this is racism does not understand what racism is. When you prefer, for a marriage candidate, somebody from your own culture and background, this is simply compatibility. Birds of a feather flock together.

Yes, if he were to say, "I'm not going to marry somebody of another race because I think they're worse than me," this and that, this is racism. And yes, in this case, go to a shaykh or wali or another person and find out the reality of what he is saying. But if a person prefers his or her own race for marriage simply because of compatibility, not because of elitism, not because of arrogance, not because of looking down at other races, this is very reasonable. And if the father were to say, "Look, I don't want to bring into my household permanently somebody that I cannot speak my language with, somebody that I'm not going to enjoy my cuisine with, somebody that cannot crack jokes in my culture," you can call it petty if you want; that's your prerogative. But it is his prerogative to have that condition as well.

So my point is: who gets to decide what is reasonable and unreasonable? Not you, with my utmost respect, because you are the one that is at the center of things. Your emotions are compromised; his emotions are compromised. We cannot expect you to step out of your position and make a fair judgment. You have emailed me (by the way, you didn't tell me, and I don't want you to tell me; I'm saying you didn't tell me the exact reasons why your father is being unreasonable), but my question is: you have used that adjective, "My father is unreasonable." Maybe he is. And if he is, and it's a reason that really does not make sense and it's going to be detrimental, then inshallah you will find a shaykh or an imam to say, "You know what..." And he will call the father, because again, it's his prerogative. He is your father; he's not a stranger to you. And he needs to be told point blank that this is wrong: "Change your mind, or else I will take over the wilayah." The imam should say that. And if he changes his mind, alhamdulillah. In any case, I hope that answers that aspect.

One other thing as well, by the way, dear sister: look, you are completely, 110%, allowed to use soft pressure, emotional pressure, on your own father. Talk to him intelligently. Tell him the goods of... why this brother is what you want, and explain to him that the pros he's bringing up are not applicable. You can appeal to him over and over and over again. You can use your own extended family: go to your cousins and aunts; maybe your mother's on your side, I don't know. Feel free to apply internal pressure and see if that is going to change his mind. Pray istikhara to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala; make du'a to Allah.

But at the end of the day, if his objection is reasonable, as decided by a third party of knowledge and of your culture, then, dear sister, he is your father, and your parents have some right over you, and inshallah he has your best interest at heart, even if you disagree with his assessment of what is your best interest. **And therefore my position would be that if it is a reasonable reason and objection, that is his prerogative, and you really do need to respect that**, or else you're going to be contravening the Sharia and perhaps potentially earning the displeasure of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. May Allah make the situation easy for you.
